title: Give me Yavneh (Gittin 56a–b)
hook: Yochanan ben Zakkai escapes the siege in a coffin and asks for a school of sages
carry: protect the small thing that lasts

segments.voice: Yesterday, a wrong invitation, a public shaming, and a city that fell. Your line was shame destroys cities.

A house is on fire, and you have maybe a minute. What do you grab? People who've lived through it often describe the same thing: not the TV, but the photos, the letters, the grandmother's ring. The small thing that carries the most. Now picture Jerusalem under Roman siege, around the year 70. Food running out. Factions fighting inside the walls. And an old teacher, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, who realizes the city may not survive, and has to decide what to carry out.
screen: `ONE MINUTE: WHAT DO YOU GRAB?` → `JERUSALEM UNDER SIEGE.` → `AN OLD TEACHER DECIDES.`

segments.voice: Tractate Gittin tells it. The zealots in the city won't let anyone leave, so Yochanan ben Zakkai pretends to be sick, then pretends to die. His students, Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua, carry him out in a coffin. At the gate the guards want to stab the body to be sure. They're talked out of it: people would say they had stabbed their own rabbi. Outside the walls, Yochanan climbs out, goes to the Roman general Vespasian, and greets him as king. Vespasian says: I'm not the king. Just then a messenger arrives from Rome: the emperor has died, and you've been made emperor. Vespasian tells the old rabbi: ask me for something. He doesn't ask to save Jerusalem. He asks: give me Yavneh and its sages. Yavneh was a small town near the coast. Along with it he asks for the family of Rabban Gamliel, and a doctor for a sage who'd fasted for years. Later sages argued about it; some said he should have asked for Jerusalem itself. The Talmud gives his reasoning: he feared if he asked too much, he'd get nothing. Historians question many details of this story. But this much is clear: after the Temple fell, Yavneh became the center where the sages gathered and kept Jewish learning alive. The Temple couldn't be saved. The school could. And from the school came the Mishnah, the Talmud, and every lesson on this part of the path.
screen: `CARRIED OUT IN A COFFIN.` · `ASK ME FOR SOMETHING.` · `GIVE ME YAVNEH AND ITS SAGES.` · `THE SCHOOL OUTLASTED THE CITY.` · then, large: `GIVE ME YAVNEH.`

segments.voice: Think of something in your life that feels big and shaky right now: a job, a plan, a situation you can't fully control. Ask the old teacher's question: if I can't save the whole thing, what's the small thing inside it that would last? A friendship, a skill, a habit, a value; name it, and picture keeping it safe.
Yavneh, the small town Yochanan ben Zakkai asked for when the Roman general offered him anything, and where Jewish learning was saved.
Your line: protect the small thing that lasts. The Temple fell; the learning didn't. That's day two hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition remembers Yavneh as the place where rabbinic Judaism was rebuilt after the Temple's destruction, and the phrase give me Yavneh is used for choosing to save what will endure.

notes: Gittin 56a–b paraphrased. The three requests: Yavneh and its sages, the dynasty of Rabban Gamliel, and physicians to heal Rabbi Tzadok. The Talmud applies Isaiah 44:25 to the choice (attributed to Rabbi Yosef or Rabbi Akiva); the script says 'later sages argued'.
Parallel in Avot de-Rabbi Natan A chapter 4; details differ.
The Vespasian-becomes-emperor scene is legend; Josephus tells a similar prophecy about himself. Historicity summarized as 'historians question many details'.
The zealots are described neutrally, as factions; the text calls them biryonei.

Audit (second sample): the teach said the students stopped the guards; in Gittin 56a the guards are talked out of it with the argument that people would say they stabbed their own rabbi (the speaker is usually read as Abba Sikra), so the line now follows the text without naming him.
